Check that an analysis recovers the truth of a fake scenario

Source: R/recovery.R
expect_recovers.Rd

expect_recovers() checks the bias, the standard error and the coverage of an estimate over the simulations of a fake scenario. It returns the assertions in the format of an expect_<scenario>() function.

Usage

expect_recovers(
  x,
  truth,
  estimate = "estimate",
  se = "se",
  lower = "lower",
  upper = "upper",
  by = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  coverage = TRUE,
  label = NULL
)

Arguments

x

The stacked results of one analysis kind, for example results$models. It is a data.frame with the column sim that save_results() adds. It has one row for each simulation, or for each simulation and group of by.

truth

The true value of the estimate. One number for every group, or a data.frame with the columns of by and a column truth, with one row for each group.

estimate, se, lower, upper

The names of the columns of x that hold the estimate, its standard error and the limits of its confidence interval.

by

NULL, or the names of the columns of x that split it into groups, for example "term". Each group gets its own assertions.

level

The level of the confidence interval of lower and upper.

coverage

TRUE checks the coverage of the interval. FALSE makes no coverage assertion and needs no lower and upper. See the section Without coverage.

label

NULL, or one string that starts the text of each assertion. NULL uses the expression of x, for example "results$models". Give a label when x is not a named object, or for two calls on one object.

Value

A data.frame with the columns assertion, expected, observed and pass, and three rows for each group, or two with coverage = FALSE. Give it to rbind() with the other assertions of the expect_<scenario>() function.

Details

expect_recovers() needs a fake scenario with random data and at least 100 simulations. A fixed scenario, for example one with values that a person computed by hand, MUST keep exact assertions that you write by hand.

The text of each assertion holds the label, the group of by, the measure and the truth, for example "results$models: bias of estimate against 0.673". The checks work on the scale of the columns. Give a log odds ratio, its standard error and its limits on the log scale, with a truth on the log scale. Do not give odds ratios. On the scale of the odds ratio, the estimate is biased, and the standard error is that of the log.

For each group and assertion, n is the number of simulations with the values that the assertion needs. The bias needs a finite estimate, the standard error a finite estimate and se, and the coverage a finite lower and upper. The empirical SE is sd(estimate) over these n simulations. z is 3.89, the two-sided normal quantile of 0.0001. The three assertions are:

  1. Bias: mean(estimate) - truth. Its Monte Carlo SE is sd(estimate) / sqrt(n). The assertion passes when |bias| <= z * MCSE.

  2. Standard error: the relative error ModSE / EmpSE - 1 of the model SE ModSE = sqrt(mean(se^2)) against the empirical SE EmpSE. Its Monte Carlo SE is (ModSE / EmpSE) * sqrt(var(se^2) / (4 * n * ModSE^4) + 1 / (2 * (n - 1))). The assertion passes when |ModSE / EmpSE - 1| <= z * MCSE.

  3. Coverage: the share of simulations where lower <= truth <= upper. The assertion passes when the share is within z * sqrt(level * (1 - level) / n) of level.

Morris, White and Crowther (2019), Table 6, define these three performance measures and give a Monte Carlo SE for each. The SE of the relative error is a delta-method approximation. It assumes that the estimate is normal, and that se is independent of the estimate. The SE of the coverage uses level, not the observed share. Under a correct analysis the true share is level, and the observed share is 1 in many small studies, which gives an SE of 0.

Each row shows the observed value, the limit and the number of simulations. It also shows "can detect": the smallest error that the assertion finds with a probability of 80% at this number of simulations. For the bias, this is (z + 0.84) * sd(estimate) / sqrt(n). For the standard error, it is the ratio ModSE / EmpSE below and above 1. For the coverage, it is the true coverage below level. A large "can detect" value means that the check passes almost anything.

The fewest simulations

An assertion fails with "too few simulations to check" when n is below:

  • 100 for the bias and the standard error. The bias uses sd(estimate), so its false-alarm probability is that of a t distribution. At 100 simulations it is 0.00018. At 30 it is 0.00054.

  • for the coverage, the smallest n that puts both limits inside 0 and 1, and at least 100. The limits are level +/- z * sqrt(level * (1 - level) / n). This is 288 for the level 0.95, and 137 for 0.9.

An assertion also fails when more than 5% of the simulations of the group miss a value that it needs. Each row shows its own number of missing simulations, also when it passes. Simulations where the model failed are not missing at random, so a pass with missing simulations is weaker.

An assertion fails on a value that cannot be right, and its row gives the count:

  • the standard error, on an se of 0 or less.

  • the coverage, on a lower above its upper.

  • the bias and the standard error, when all estimates are equal. The Monte Carlo SE is then 0.

Without coverage

With coverage = FALSE, expect_recovers() checks the bias and the standard error only. It gives no row for the coverage, so the coverage is not checked, and x needs no columns lower and upper. Each assertion then needs 100 simulations. Use it for a simulation that is too slow for 288 simulations, the number that the coverage of a 95% interval needs. Use it also for an analysis without a confidence interval. The bias and the standard error are the same as with coverage = TRUE.

The false alarms

A false alarm is a failed assertion for a correct analysis. It stops the run, and the same seeds give it again in the next run. So z is large. For each assertion the probability is about 0.0001. For one call with g groups and 3 assertions in each group, it is about 1 - (1 - 0.0001)^(3 * g):

GroupsAssertionsFalse alarm of the call
130.0003
6180.0018
20600.0060

The real probabilities are a little larger, because the bias is a t statistic and the coverage is a binomial count. At 300 simulations, the bias has 0.00012 and the coverage at the level 0.95 has 0.00028. There is no option to change z.

References

Morris TP, White IR, Crowther MJ. Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine. 2019;38:2074-2102. doi:10.1002/sim.8086

See also

expect_biased() for a control analysis, and vignette("pbn").

Other checks of fake scenarios: expect_biased()

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- data.frame(sim = 1:300, estimate = rnorm(300, 0.5, 0.2), se = 0.2)
x$lower <- x$estimate - 1.96 * x$se
x$upper <- x$estimate + 1.96 * x$se
pbn::expect_recovers(x, truth = 0.5)
#>                                assertion
#> 1        x: bias of estimate against 0.5
#> 2 x: model SE of estimate against its SD
#> 3 x: coverage of 0.5 by the 95% interval
#>                                                                         expected
#> 1                      |bias| <= 0.0433 (3.89 MCSE); can detect |bias| of 0.0527
#> 2 |relative error| <= 16.5% (3.89 MCSE); can detect ModSE/EmpSE of 0.834 or 1.23
#> 3                       0.901 to 0.999 (3.89 MCSE); can detect coverage of 0.886
#>                                                 observed pass
#> 1                        0.00672; 300 of 300 simulations TRUE
#> 2 +3.8% (ModSE 0.2, EmpSE 0.193); 300 of 300 simulations TRUE
#> 3                          0.947; 300 of 300 simulations TRUE
